title: Nakamura Breaks Calendar Record With 4th Consecutive Victory
summary: In a week when GM Hikaru Nakamura pushed Chess.com's blitz record to new heights, it is fitting that he also broke the record for the most Bullet Brawl victories in a single year, albeit with three months to spare. A dominant run in the second half of the two-hour arena saw Nakamura claim the $400 first prize for the fourth week in a row with a score of 155. GMs Jose Martinez, Tuan Minh Le, and Pranav Venkatesh finished second through fourth and earned themselves $250, $150, and $100, respectively, while IMs Renato Terry and Havard Haug were unlucky to miss out on prize money due to inferior tiebreaks. Meanwhile, IM Rose Atwell won the $100 best women's prize. The next edition of Bullet Brawl will begin on Saturday, October 10, at 12 p.m. ET / 18:00 CEST / 9:30 p.m. IST. Standings

title: Awonder Liang Invincible At Seirawan Chess, The Complex Variant
summary: GM Awonder Liang blanked his opposition with 3-0 victories in all the matches to convincingly win the 2026 Seirawan Chess Championship, an event he won in 2024 too. It was a brisk evening for the 23-year-old American GM, who was hardly in any trouble in all 12 games, which he won, pocketing the $750 first prize in quick time. 20-year-old FM Jakub Chyzy of Poland, who lost to him in both the Winners Final and the Grand Final, finished second to earn $500. Comparatively, the Seirawan Chess variant comes across as a tougher version of chess to play. Four pieces get added in the middlegame in total, making the chessboard a crowded place, giving rise to more tactical possibilities. Eight pieces can potentially act as knights in the middlegame, which makes a lot of hopping around of pieces on the board. At the same time, the elephant and the hawk are a rook and a bishop too, respectively. And finally, there is the difficulty in assessing the imbalance of piece equations with respect to the elephant and the queen, especially in the blitz time control of three minutes per player plus a two-second increment each move. All this makes the variant tough to play and delightful but complicated to spectate. As you will see, it is especially in judging the imbalance that Liang showed his class, apart from his tactical prowess. All eight players who reached the finals through the qualifiers in the previous two days finished on the prize list: Ionatan Giurgiu lost to Liang in the Winners Semifinal and to Chyzy in the Losers Final to finish third for $350, FM Vladislav Lymar was fourth for $250, Patrik Saar and Hugo Zanotti Caetano both fifth and sixth for $175, and Arian Rahimpour and Christiaan Smeets seventh and eighth for $100 each. The variant is an invention of GM Yasser Seirawan and FM Bruce Harper, with both sides getting two extra pieces, the hawk and the elephant. The hawk is a combination of a bishop and knight, while the elephant combines a rook and knight. Neither piece is present on the board when the game starts and are introduced into play by choice at any square on the first rank when they get vacant with the moving away of any of the original occupants. They cannot be introduced into play if all the pieces get developed from the first rank. They can also be conjured up by pawn promotions. All the other rules of chess remain the same as the original. The tournament was an eight-player double-elimination with each match played as the best of four games. The time control was 3+2, and decided by a sudden-death 1+2 tiebreak game in case of a match getting tied. The following players reached the Finals from the eight qualifiers on the initial two days. Liang raced through the Winners Bracket with clean 3-0 sweeps in all the matches. His tactical strength was his obvious forte, which he showed in his very first game of the day, in the Winners Quarterfinal against Patrik Saar. With just seven seconds remaining on his clock, Liang spotted the elegant 32.He7+! here. Once you understand the basis of the combination, you can work out that 32...Kf8 is not legal here, as the hawk on e7 protects the f8-square too. In case of 32...Kh8, White plays 33.Qa8+ Kh7 34.Qg8#, with the queen supported by the hawk on e7. Though he was materially down in the second, he won that and the next too, to wrap up the match with a 3-0 score. Another 3-0 score followed in the Semifinals against Giurgiu, with the second game of the match showcasing Liang's tactical prowess. In the same move, Liang got his bishop to h3, attacking the g2-point, as well as introducing the hawk on c8. After 15.g3, he used the just-born hawk immediately with 15...Hg4!, uncorking the combination 16.Exh4 Exh4 17.gxh4 Hf3+! checkmate which won him the game. Try to spend a minute with the position to understand the combination and appreciate Liang's tactical skill. In the Final against Chyzy, Liang's understanding of the variant shone through in the very first game. Chyzy has just played 19...He5, and Liang decided to trade his queen for the hawk with 20.Qxe5. (We are still not sure if we should use the word 'sacrifice' here.) Even the commentators weren't really convinced by the trade and had assumed that Liang's position was worse but, on the contrary, he steadily built up an attack on the kingside and finally won the game on move 53. He won the match 3-0, once again. After losing to Liang, Chyzy went to the Losers Bracket and directly played the final against Giurgiu. In the very first game, he found a neat combination involving a couple of sacrifices and a knight fork to score an elegant win. Here, Chyzy uncorked the delightful 21...Bxf2! 22.Rxf2 Rh1+!! 23.Kxh1 Nxf2+ 24.Kg1 Nxd1, winning the white queen. For the purists of the game, it is somewhat heartening that none of the involved pieces were from the variant. He won the match with a 3-0 score. The Grand Final proved to be anticlimactic, with Liang extending his domination a notch higher with another 3-0 win against Chyzy. A curious moment occurred in the very first game of the match. For the previous two moves, the spectators had to survive the anxiety of wondering why White wouldn't capture Exd7 before realizing that the white elephant on e5 (is that a pun?) may actually be stronger than the black queen on d7. But then, Black's 13...g6?? was an unfortunate blunder, overlooking that the elephant is actually a rook too. White followed up with the obvious 14.Qxf6, exploiting the white elephant's pinning the e7-pawn to the black king, thus not allowing the capture 14...exf6. Liang went on to win the game soon. Considering that Chyzy wouldn't have been too tired by this point, his tactical oversight must only be attributed to the elephant's capabilities simply not getting recognized on the board. The next game featured a cute 'shot' from Liang. Liang goes in for the kill with 24...Bf3!! In fact, he had an even stronger resource in 24...Bxg2!! The tactic behind the sacrifice is that, after the natural 25.gxf3, Black continues 25...Qxh3, with a strong mating attack thanks to the hawk on d6, which casts its evil eye on the h2-square. Chyzy responded with 25.Qxf3 and White was soon lost after 25...Exf3 26.gxf3 Rxf3 with a strong attack still intact. Two more Community Chess Championships remain to be played in 2026, Crazyhouse and Fog of War. How to rewatch? You could watch the broadcast on the Chess.com Community Twitch and YouTube channels. Results and info can be found on our dedicated events page. The live broadcast was hosted by Seirawan and Harper, the creators of the variant.

title: Critical thinking takes centre stage at Judit Polgar's Global Chess Festival
summary:
More than a conventional chess event

The 12 th Judit Polgar Global Chess Festival took place at the Hungarian National Gallery in Budapest on Saturday 26 September. Founded in 2015, the annual event again combined tournament chess with education, art, technology and activities aimed at families and younger visitors. The theme chosen for the 2026 edition was Critical Thinking , with much of the programme exploring how chess can be used to analyse information, test assumptions and make decisions.

The festival has gradually expanded beyond the framework of a conventional chess event. Earlier editions have included simultaneous exhibitions, professional competitions, conferences, artistic projects and programmes connecting chess with science and technology.

In 2018, events linked to the festival were held at 250 venues in 23 countries, while the main gathering had already moved to the Hungarian National Gallery. Subsequent editions introduced conferences on chess and education, hybrid activities and discussions about artificial intelligence.

The event was held online in 2020 and in hybrid form in subsequent years before returning to a larger programme of on-site activities. Recent editions have addressed subjects including women in chess and science, decision-making and the relationship between chess and artificial intelligence.

Attracting potential new generations of chess players! | Photos: Global Chess Festival

Chess, education and artificial intelligence

This year's programme ran from 10:00 to 17:30 and included both all-day activities and events at fixed times. Among the former were the Master Relay Simul, Live Chess Painting, the Chess Palace Adventure Trail, logic activities and opportunities for visitors to challenge experienced players. Timed events included tournaments, educational sessions, robot programming and a screening of the documentary Queen of Chess .

Several activities were directly connected to the festival's central theme. A session on Chess Palace and artificial intelligence in education was accompanied by programmes aimed at parents, while the main stage included a demonstration in which chess players faced AI models designed to reproduce aspects of their playing style. Other activities focused on observation, logic and distinguishing reliable information from misleading impressions.

Polgar also played a blindfold game against Hungarian grandmaster Gergely Antal, which ended in a draw. Her sister Sofia Polgar was among the guests and took part alongside Judit and GM Krisztian Szabo in the Master Relay Simul, in which several masters alternated in continuing the same games.

Sofia Polgar showing the moves of the blindfold encounter between her sister Judit and Gergely Antal | Photo: Global Chess Festival

Two of the three Polgar sisters met in Budapest | Photo: Global Chess Festival

Five communities face Polgar

One of the main chess events of the day was the Community Chess Simul, staged on the first floor of the National Gallery. Rather than playing individual opponents in the usual simultaneous format, Polgar faced five communities, whose representatives could receive ideas and analysis from members following remotely. The event was broadcast online and hosted by IM Anna Rudolf.

Polgar finished the exhibition with 3½ points from 5 games , recording three wins, one draw and one defeat. Her only loss came against the Pietro Chess community, while the Chess Is For Everyone team held her to a draw. The other three encounters ended in Polgar's favour. The Hungarian Stars team, a group of intellectuals headed by neuroscientist Szilveszter E. Vizi, was unusual in that it played without assistance from an online community.

The format continued an idea used in previous editions of the festival: combining players physically present in Budapest with much larger groups taking part remotely. The 2024 festival had already featured a hybrid community simul, while the 2026 version placed the participating groups directly opposite Polgar on five boards.

Judit Polgar shakes hands with Australian streamer Hannah Sayce ahead of their encounter (Sayce played with the help of her online community) | Photo: Global Chess Festival

Neuroscientist Szilveszter E. Vizi leading the Hungarian Stars team in the simultaneous exhibition | Photo: Global Chess Festival

All games - Community Simul

Chess meets the Rubik's Cube

Another distinctive part of the programme was the RubikChess Tournament , which was opened to the general public for the first time. Organised in cooperation with the FIDE Commission for Women's Chess and with support from Rubik's, the competition brought together two activities closely associated with logic and pattern recognition.

Players competed in two-person teams over five rounds. In each round, one member played chess while the other solved a 3×3 Rubik's Cube, with the teams deciding beforehand which player would perform each task. The event was aimed primarily at amateur chess players, with a maximum rating of 1800, as well as cube enthusiasts. Ernő Rubik and Sofia Polgar were present for the opening.

The tournament followed the introduction of RubikChess at the previous festival and was also represented on the main stage, where winners of the first competition demonstrated the format with commentary from Judit Polgar.

Rubik's Cube meets chess in Budapest | Photo: Global Chess Festival

The RubikChess Tournament in progress | Photo: Global Chess Festival

title: From Tsaghkadzor to the Grand Final: European Schools Chess Champions crowned amidst cultural celebration
summary:
Press release by FIDE

The curtain fell on the World Schools Team Championship Europe 2026. After four days of intense competition, brilliant sacrifices, and unparalleled teamwork, the young chess champions were crowned in Tsaghkadzor, Armenia.

Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk (Belarus) established their dominance from the opening round. Starting with back-to-back 4–0 clean sweeps, they held a firm grasp on the number-one spot. Led by Board 1 star Damir Bulgak and Board 4 standout Katrina Yakovleva, the Belarusian squad never let their grip slip, successfully turning away all challengers to finish with a flawless, undefeated record. Their first-place finish officially secures their slot in the prestigious global Grand Final this December.

Coming into the event as the top-seeded team by average rating, Riga State Gymnasium No. 1 (Latvia) confidently navigated eight rounds, losing only to the champions and winning all their other encounters. Powered by Daniel Beniosev's unbeaten run on Board 2, the Latvians easily defended their position down the stretch to lock up the silver medals.

LEPL Georgia, Kutaisi Andria Razmadze Physico secured the third position in a tough competition with the local team from Armenia.

Final standings

...27 teams

Let's take a look at how the action unfolded on the final day of the competition.

Round 7

Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk further consolidated its lead, scoring a hard-fought victory over ZS Wolkerova Bardejov. Meanwhile, in the clash of the teams chasing the leaders, Riga State Gymnasium No. 1 dominated LEPL Georgia, Kutaisi Andria Razmadze Physico by a score of 3-1.

Move of the day

Matej Viglas – Damir Bulgak

Leading up to move 26, Black emerged clearly better, but there was nothing decisive in sight after the correct 26.Ne5 f6 27.Nd3. However, White committed a fatal error with 26.Nd2?? , walking right into a devastating tactical strike. The knight sacrifice 26…Nxf2! completely shattered White's kingside shelter. Accepting the sacrifice leads to a forced checkmate after 27.Kxf2 Qxh2+ 28.Kf1 Re6! , while declining it leaves White completely lost. The rest was smooth sailing for Bulgak.

Round 8

Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk finished with a perfect match score after defeating Green Village School of Israel. Riga State Gymnasium No.1 swept Osnovna sola Bojana Ilicha Maribor, while in the crucial match for third place LEPL Georgia, Kutaisi Andria Razmadze Physico prevailed over the local team Yerevan’s basic school N 77.

A web of friendships

Beyond the intense chess battles on the chessboards of Tsaghkadzor, the World Schools Team Championship 2026 celebrated the power of global connection through a deeply symbolic "Threads that connect" side event. In this heartwarming activity, young chess prodigies from across Europe stood in a large circle, sharing their reflections and tossing colorful balls of yarn across the room while holding onto their piece of the string. As the yarn traveled from hand to hand, it created a magnificent, intricate web, a striking, tangible visualization of international networking and shared community. This playful yet profound exercise beautifully reminded our future grandmasters that just like their strategic choices on the board, their paths, cultures, and newfound friendships are all interconnected in one grand, supportive network.

The European Stage World Schools Team Championship 2026 concluded with an unforgettable, high-energy closing ceremony hosted at the 88 Hotel & Spa. Bringing together young players, captains, parents, and international chess dignitaries, the event celebrated four days of intense boundary-crossing competition, ultimate triumphs, and cross-cultural camaraderie.

The Master of Ceremonies opened the evening by thanking the young players for building friendships across borders, emphasizing that the global chess community is “one big family.” Special recognition was paid to Freedom Group of companies, the event's main sponsor and General Partner of the International School Chess Federation (ISCF). The MC also expressed deep appreciation to the tournament's key co-organizers: the Armenian Chess Federation, the Chess Academy of Armenia, the European Chess Union, and the venue host, 88 Hotel & Spa.

The official segment of the evening began with the national anthem of Armenia. The audience remained respectfully standing before the proceedings transitioned seamlessly into the official FIDE anthem. Following the protocols, the energy in the hall skyrocketed during the screening of the tournament's highlight film, titled "How It All Happened". Young players filled the room with thunderous shouts and laughter, following the MC's prompt to "make some noise" whenever they spotted themselves on screen.

Individual board triumphs

Chief Arbiter Vahagn Khachatryan took the stage to announce the individual category medalists, who were presented their awards by an esteemed lineup of academic and chess royalty.

Reserve Board awards were presented by Mariam Ispiryan, Pro-rector of the Armenian State Pedagogical University.

Lile Svanadze from LEPL Georgia and Kutaisi Andria Razmadze from Physico-Mathematical Public School N41

Catalan Julen Arbizu from Ikastola San Fermin

Maksymilian Wylezinski from Azymut Szkola Podstawowa Fundacji Sternik

Board 4 awards were presented by Grandmaster and Honored Coach of Armenia, Arman Pashikyan.

loana-Cristiana Pomirleanu from C.N. Costache Negruzzi

Katrina Yakovleva from Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk

Adam Ben Avi from Green Village School

Board 3 awards were presented by Varduhi Sargsyan, Executive Director of the Chess Academy of Armenia

Krisjanis Lazars from Riga State Gymnasium No. 1

Platon Kiritshenko from Tallinna Tonismae Reaalkool

Kiryl Babeikin from Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk

Board 2 awards were presented by Lilit Mkrtchyan, Rector of the Armenian State Pedagogical University

Daniel Beniosev from Riga State Gymnasium No. 1

Mikita Mazanik from Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk

Adrian Kornilov from Tallinna Tonismae Reaalkool

Board 1 awards were presented by Ion-Serban Dobronauteanu, Director of Youth Chess of the European Chess Union.

Damir Bulgak from Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk

Tin Biti from OS Spansko Oranice

Uros Vuckovic from Mathematical Grammar School

Following the individual honors, the Tournament Director of the FIDE ISCF World Schools Team Championships 2026, Nadzeya Krauchuk, delivered a brief address congratulating the field on their tactical excellence.

The podium

The culmination of the 60-minute ceremony belonged to the three best school teams in Europe, who took their places on the podium to thunderous applause.

Smbat Lputian, founder of the Chess Academy of Armenia and Vice President of the Armenian Chess Federation, presented the bronze medals, trophy, and certificates to LEPL Georgia, Kutaisi Andria Razmadze Physico.

Zurab Azmaiparashvili, President of the European Chess Union, called up the silver medalists from Riga State Gymnasium No. 1 to accept their team trophy.

To crown the ultimate champions, 7th FIDE President Arkady Dvorkovich took the stage to welcome the undefeated European Continental Champions: Minsk Gymnasium No. 50. The hall stood for a passionate rendition of the winning team's national anthem, accompanied by a standing ovation, fireworks, and the iconic strains of "We Are the Champions".

Cultural farewell and party time

To capture the true heartbeat of the host country, the evening concluded with a stunning exhibition of traditional Armenian dance, showcasing the deep roots and breathtaking spirit of the local culture.

With the European chapter now officially closed, the top-qualified teams from all four Continental Stages are shifting their focus to the upcoming Grand Final this December.
